title: Why did Jesus have to die?
summary: Sin is not just a list of bad deeds, but a broken bond with God - lost trust, out of which specific sins grow. The result is separation and death, and God's answer is the cross: Jesus took my place to restore the relationship. Obedience is the fruit of reconciliation, not its condition.

sections.heading: Sin is, above all, a broken bond

items.comment: The essence of sin is separation: "your iniquities are what separate you from God". The problem is not first a broken rule, but lost closeness.

questions.text: Have you thought of sin so far more as "breaking a rule" or as "breaking a relationship"? What does this second perspective change?

items.comment: The first effect of sin is not punishment, but hiding and fear of God. The human being runs from the One with whom he had walked in closeness.

questions.text: Why did the human being, after sin, begin to fear God and hide from him, instead of running to him?

items.comment: Sin (singular) is described as a direction: "each of us has turned to his own way". It is self-centeredness, a turning away from God toward oneself.

questions.text: How do you recognize in yourself the tendency to "go your own way" instead of God's - even when no one is watching?

items.comment: Jesus defines sin at its deepest: "sin... that they do not believe in me". The root is a lack of trust in God, not a single bad deed.

questions.text: Why can a lack of trust in God be a deeper problem than specific bad deeds?

items.label: "sin" as missing the target
items.content: The most common biblical word for sin (Hebrew *chatta't*, Greek *hamartia*) carries the image of "missing the target, falling short of the goal". The human being's goal is a life of trust and relationship with God (cf. John 16:9); sin (singular) is missing this goal - a broken bond, out of which the individual sins (plural) only then arise. That is why the Gospel first heals the relationship, rather than only correcting behavior.

questions.text: How does the image of "missing the target, which is relationship with God" order our understanding of sin as a state, and not just a series of acts?

sections.heading: Sin (singular) and sins (plural): root and fruit

items.comment: Bad deeds ("sins", plural) flow "from within, from the heart". They are symptoms of the illness, not the illness itself - the fruit of a corrupted root.

questions.text: What would change if we healed the "root" (the heart), instead of only fighting individual "fruits"?

items.label: three Hebrew words for sin
items.content: The Old Testament describes sin with three main words that together convey its fullness: *chatta't* (missing the target), *pesza* (rebellion, a deliberate transgression, the breaking of a relationship with authority) and *awon* (a twisting, guilt, the "bending" of what was meant to be straight). Sin is therefore at once a mistake, a rebellion and a distortion - not only an "error", but a wounding of the relationship on several levels.

items.comment: The human heart is "deceitful" and will not heal itself. That is why the problem of sin cannot be solved by mere improvement of behavior.

questions.text: Why is "trying harder" not enough if the problem sits in the heart, and not only in our deeds?

items.label: sin "is crouching at the door" (Gen 4:7)
items.content: Right before the first murder, God warns Cain that sin "lies at the door" and "crouches" for him - the image of a predator ready to pounce, which he must "master". It is one of the first descriptions in the Bible of sin as a hostile force, not just a single act: something that wants to "get" us and subdue us, rather than a neutral "mistake".

questions.text: What does it change in the fight against temptation to picture sin as a "crouching predator" that you must master before it masters you?

items.comment: Even Paul confesses the inner split: "I do not do the good I want". It is a description of human helplessness before sin as a force, not just a series of mistakes.

questions.text: Do you know that experience of "I want to do well, but it turns out otherwise"? What does it say about our need for help from outside?

items.comment: "All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God." The problem is universal - no one stands outside it, and no one can save himself.

questions.text: What does it give you to realize that in the problem of sin we are all "on equal footing" and all need the same grace?

items.label: "redemption" as a buying back from slavery (Rom 3:24)
items.content: Right after "all have sinned" comes the solution: justified "through the redemption that is in Christ". The Greek *apolytrōsis* is an image from the market of slaves and captives: the buying of someone into freedom for a price paid. Sin is therefore not just a "debt on an account", but a slavery we cannot get out of by ourselves - we need Someone to pay the ransom and lead us out into freedom.

items.comment: "The wages of sin is death" - the natural consequence of being cut off from the Giver of life. But the same sentence also speaks of a "gift": eternal life in Christ.

questions.text: Why is death a "consequence" of separation from God, and not just an arbitrary punishment?

items.label: "wages" is a soldier's pay (Rom 6:23)
items.content: The word rendered as "wages" (Greek *opsōnion*) meant the pay given to a soldier - what is owed to someone for service. Sin "is owed" death as its earned consequence. Paul deliberately sets this against the second half of the verse: eternal life is not "pay", but *charisma* - a gift of grace. One is earned, the other can only be received.

items.comment: God takes sin seriously - he does not make light of it. Breaking with Life leads to death; this is not a "trifle to be overlooked".

questions.text: How do you reconcile God being love with his taking sin with deadly seriousness?

items.comment: Even our "righteous deeds" will not bridge the chasm - in themselves they are "like a polluted garment". We need someone to build the bridge from the other side.

questions.text: What does it mean that a broken relationship with God cannot be bought back with "good deeds"?

sections.heading: The cross: Jesus took my place

items.comment: God did not wait until we improved. "While we were still sinners, Christ died for us" - the initiative is on God's side.

questions.text: What does it say about God that he came forward with the solution before we ever asked for it?

items.comment: "He was pierced for our transgressions... and by his wounds we are healed." Jesus voluntarily took upon himself the consequence that was owed to us.

questions.text: How do you feel reading that the suffering owed to you was taken on by Someone else - voluntarily?

items.label: the song of the suffering Servant (Isa 52:13-53:12)
items.content: Isa 53 is one of the "Servant Songs". It describes Someone who suffers not for his own guilt, but "for our transgressions", and through this "justifies" many. The New Testament reads this passage directly as referring to Jesus (for example Acts 8:32-35; 1 Pet 2:22-25). It is one of the strongest bridges between the Old Testament and the cross: substitutionary suffering announced centuries before Golgotha.

questions.text: What does it mean that God's answer to sin - a Servant suffering in our place - was announced long before the cross?

items.comment: Jesus "in his body bore our sins on the tree" - so that we might "die to sin and live to righteousness". The cross not only forgives, but sets free.

questions.text: What is the difference between forgiveness that merely "cancels the guilt" and forgiveness that sets you free for a new life?

items.label: "cursed on the tree" (1 Pet 2:24)
items.content: The expression "bore our sins on the tree" reaches back to Deut 21:23: "cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree". Paul applies this directly to the cross: "Christ redeemed us... having become a curse for us" (Gal 3:13). Jesus took not only our place in death, but also the "curse" owed to sin - so that the blessing might flow down to us.

items.comment: The great exchange: the Sinless One "became sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God". He takes what is mine, I receive what is his.

questions.text: What does it mean to you that on the cross an "exchange" took place: my guilt for his righteousness?

items.label: the cross and the Day of Atonement (propitiation)
items.content: The background of the "exchange" in 2 Cor 5:21 is the Old Testament Day of Atonement (Lev 16): the people's sin was symbolically transferred onto the sacrifice, and the blood was brought into the most holy place. The New Testament calls Jesus "the propitiation" (Greek *hilastērion* - the same word the Septuagint uses for the "mercy seat", the lid of the Ark where atonement was made, Rom 3:25). The cross is the fulfillment of what the sanctuary only foreshadowed.

items.comment: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends." The cross is the supreme proof of love, not of anger.

questions.text: How does the fact that the cross is a proof of love (and not of God's anger) change the picture of all of Christianity?

items.comment: At the heart of the cross is "reconciliation" - God "does not count people's trespasses against them" and restores the broken bond. The goal is relationship, not just a clean record.

questions.text: What does a person need most: a "clean record" or a restored relationship? Can you have one without the other?

items.label: "reconciliation": turning hostility into friendship
items.content: The Greek *katallagē* ("reconciliation") comes from the language of relationship and means turning hostility into friendship, the restoring of a broken bond. In 2 Cor 5:18-19 the active party is God: it is he who reconciles us to himself. The cross does not "persuade" a reluctant God to love us - on the contrary, it is the expression of the love of a God who already loves us and, at his own cost, removes what divides us.

questions.text: Why does it matter that it is God who reconciles us to himself, rather than us having to "appease" a reluctant God?

items.comment: The fruit of justification by faith is "peace with God". The hostility is over; we can again walk with him without fear.

questions.text: What does it practically change in everyday life to live "at peace with God", rather than in fear of him?

items.comment: It is "grace... that teaches us" to reject evil and live well. Obedience is the fruit of grace received, not a price that must be paid to obtain it.

questions.text: Why is obedience that grows out of gratitude different from obedience out of fear or out of a desire to "earn it"?

items.comment: "We love because he first loved us." The whole order is this: first love received, then a response with one's life.

questions.text: How does the motivation for a good life change when it begins with "he first loved me"?

application.text: Sin is not first a list of offenses, but a broken bond - lost trust in God, out of which specific sins grow. The result is separation and death, because apart from the Giver of life there is no life. But God did not leave us on the other side of the chasm: on the cross Jesus took my place, took upon himself the consequence of sin and opened the way of reconciliation. I do not have to improve first for God to accept me - that acceptance is the starting point, and obedience its fruit.
application.challenge: This week, stand before the cross with one specific "sin" (a deed) and with a question about its root: where did I lack trust in God? Tell Jesus directly that you accept what he did in your place, and ask not so much to "be better" as for restored closeness. Write down one thing you want to give to God as the first fruit of this relationship.
